question_details.description:
This question is synced with an identical question on Metaculus. The original question opened on 2023-08-26 19:59:00 and can be found [here](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/18541). This question will resolve to the same value as the synced question. The original question's background info at this time is below. 

As of August 2023, China has only one military base overseas - a naval base in Djibouti, Africa. However, there are clear indications that they are interested in expanding their global power projection capabilities, and indeed some overseas naval bases are allegedly under construction in Asia and Africa.

With the adding of seven new member countries to BRICS, an alliance primarily focused on economic and diplomatic partnership, it is an important question regarding the standoff between East and West whether BRICS will take a more militaristic aspect as well. Overseas Chinese military bases would be a strong indication of this.

[China may be planning overseas naval bases] https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/jul/27/china-building-overseas-naval-bases-across-asia-and-africa-say-analysts

question_details.resolution_criteria:
The question will resolve to YES if either the Chinese government or US intelligence community publicly announces a Chinese military base in a BRICS country before January 1st, 2026.

The country needs to be an official member of BRICS, thus the seven new nations that were invited in August 2023 will count towards YES only after January 2024, when they're projected to officially join.

If the Chinese base is in a country which only afterwards joins BRICS, the question will still resolve to YES.
question_details.fine_print:
US intelligence community's announcement requires a "high likelihood of Chinese operated base". In the event of numerical announcement (which is unlikely), "high likelihood" means a confidence of 90% or more.

The base needs to be projected to operate indefinitely, meaning that the Chinese operating a military base for the duration of temporary exercises (<1 year) do not count towards YES.

Naval bases and a military airfields both count as military bases.

Announcement from Pentagon or a US government institution of equal significance (e.g. White House) counts as Intelligence Community announcement.

**Beaches or Bases?**
China's coastal investments in Pakistan under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) are framed as tourism and leisure development—featuring beach resorts, marinas, and eco-villages—but serve strategic military and logistical purposes. Key coastal nodes from Keti Bandar to Jiwani are designed as dual-use facilities, with Gwadar serving as the central command hub. According to The Diplomat (2024), these developments form a 'maritime necklace' where commercial and military functions overlap. Gwadar’s deep-sea port, operated by China Overseas Ports Holding Company under a 40-year lease, hosts luxury zones and smart city infrastructure, aligning with China’s civil-military fusion doctrine. Satellite imagery from Reuters (2023) shows restricted zones and expanded berthing capacity, suggesting military readiness. Precedents in Hambantota (Sri Lanka), Sihanoukville (Cambodia), and Djibouti demonstrate how Chinese-financed projects evolve into strategic footholds. Pakistan’s external debt to China exceeds US $30 billion, with coastal projects increasing dependency. Chinese-funded surveillance systems by Huawei and Dahua Technologies raise cybersecurity concerns, with data potentially accessible to the Chinese state (CSIS, 2024). Environmental damage from dredging and reclamation threatens fragile ecosystems, fueling local resentment. Displacement of fishing communities and minimal compensation have led to 'alienated modernity,' where residents see development but not benefit. Military utility is evident: tourist infrastructure can host naval vessels, fiber-optic cables support secure communications, and airstrips can serve drones. Regional powers like India, Iran, and Gulf states view CPEC’s maritime reach as a challenge to their strategic interests. The article argues that China’s strategy blends soft power—bilingual signage, cultural festivals, and urban design resembling Shenzhen—with psychological framing to normalize its presence. Experts from Brookings and Carnegie recommend joint control, independent audits, and diversified partnerships to balance leverage. Ultimately, the article concludes that CPEC’s 'beaches' are not leisure destinations but strategic beachheads, where development and dependency are intertwined.

**'Hundreds of Soldiers and Nuclear Ships': Details of Sudan's Proposal to Russia for Its First African Naval Base**
The Sudanese military government has proposed a 25-year agreement to Russia, according to a report by 'The Wall Street Journal' citing Sudanese officials, allowing Moscow to establish its first naval base in Africa on the Red Sea. Under the proposal, Russia could deploy up to 300 soldiers, anchor four warships—including nuclear-powered vessels—and gain preferential access to Sudanese mining contracts, especially for gold. The base in Port Sudan would enable Russia to monitor maritime traffic toward the Suez Canal, through which approximately 12% of global trade passes. In return, Sudan would receive advanced Russian air defense systems and weapons at preferential prices to support its war against the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). However, a Sudanese official warned the deal could provoke tensions with the United States and the European Union. U.S. officials are concerned that such a base would expand Russia’s naval presence and military operations in the Red Sea, Mediterranean, and Indian Ocean. Moscow has sought permanent access to Port Sudan for five years, and Russian forces are already present in several African countries. Experts believe the agreement would be a major strategic gain for Russian President Vladimir Putin. Meanwhile, China has built ports across Africa and operates a naval base in Djibouti near the largest U.S. base on the continent, while the U.S. maintains military presence in Somalia. Russia’s influence in Africa has declined since the dismantling of the Wagner Group and the death of its founder Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2023, making the Sudanese conflict a new opportunity. Initially, Russia supported the RSF to gain access to Sudan’s gold, but later shifted allegiance to support the Sudanese government. In parallel, the Sudanese military has acquired drones from Iran, Egypt, and Turkey. Analysts suggest the military’s push to finalize the deal reflects the deteriorating state of its military position: despite controlling Khartoum, the RSF has fully seized Darfur, with reports of new massacres against civilians. The war has killed around 150,000 people and displaced 12 million, constituting one of Africa’s worst humanitarian crises.

Organizational challenges persist, including poor interservice integration and difficulties integrating advanced technologies like hypersonic weapons and AI into a cohesive, real-time command-and-control system. Additionally, China faces intense political pressure to meet ambitious timelines—2027 for initial capability, 2035 for full modernization, and 2049 for 'world-class' status—which may lead to premature deployment of underdeveloped systems. While China has made remarkable progress in individual capabilities, the integration of these systems into a combat-tested, globally deployable force remains unproven. The U.S. retains enduring advantages in power projection, nuclear readiness, joint operations, and alliance cohesion. However, the gap is expected to narrow over time due to China’s methodical modernization strategy.

The 17th BRICS Summit in Rio de Janeiro (July 2025) addressed global health, infrastructure finance, climate, AI governance, and security reform. While BRICS members jointly criticized Western hegemony, they avoided firm commitments on a common currency or alternative reserve system.
